rubric.label: Real pain
rubric.help: Do people already spend money or hours on this problem today?

rubric.label: Clear payer
rubric.help: Can you name who pays, and roughly how much?

rubric.label: Your edge
rubric.help: What do you have that a random competitor doesn't (skills, access, network, taste)?

rubric.label: Room in market
rubric.help: 5 = wide open, 1 = crowded with cheap or free substitutes.

rubric.label: Speed to first krona
rubric.help: 5 = could get paid within a month, 1 = a year or more.

rubric.label: Life fit
rubric.help: Does it suit your job, the Vietnam stint, your writing and energy?

stages.name: Hunch
stages.test: Write the one-sentence pitch: who, what pain, what they pay.

stages.name: Desk research
stages.test: Competitors, prices and substitutes mapped. Rubric scored honestly.

stages.name: Conversations
stages.test: Five real potential buyers talked to. At least two say 'I'd pay for that' unprompted.

stages.name: Smoke test
stages.test: A concrete offer with a price is put in front of people (page, DM, pitch). Someone tries to buy.

stages.name: First money
stages.test: One paying customer, at a price that isn't a favour.

stages.name: Survived
stages.test: Repeatable: a second and third customer came without heroic effort.

ideas.name: AI adoption for small teams
ideas.pitch: Workshops, workflow redesign and small internal tools for 20–250 person companies that pay for AI tools but don't use them well.
ideas.verdict: The struggle is real and measurable: two thirds of Swedish firms use no AI, and those that hold back cite lack of expertise first. The market is crowded at the enterprise top and at the cheap-freelancer bottom. The durable product isn't tool tips, which go stale monthly, but workflow redesign, policy and an ongoing retainer to keep a team current. Knowledge going stale is the reason a retainer makes sense, not a reason to avoid this. Expect a 3–5 year window before tools get easy enough that small firms can do it themselves.
edge: Real building track record: CV app, review tools, footage pipelines, event sites
Video production and events background, a niche you can speak to credibly
Swedish and Vietnamese, plus access to Vietnamese-Swedish business owners
Your own workplace can be the first case study

competitors.who: Accenture, Deloitte, PwC, EY, KPMG, Capgemini/Sogeti, Knowit, Netlight, Tietoevry
competitors.note: Enterprise budgets (hundreds of thousands of SEK and up). Rarely bother with a 15-person company.

competitors.who: Alice Labs, PhaseOne.ai, Lampo AI Automation, Opsio, Nytta AI (Växjö)
competitors.note: A data vendor counts about 192 AI consulting firms based in Sweden (Aug 2026), with Stockholm the largest hub. Several target SMEs directly.

competitors.who: NobleProg, Active Solution, Hyper Island and Berghs courses, Microsoft Copilot partners
competitors.note: Workshops and courses, often generic and not built around the client's own tasks.
AI & ML is one of Upwork's most-bid subcategories. n8n specialists charge roughly $40–100/h. Price pressure is strong here.

competitors.who: YouTube, an internal 'AI champion', the vendors' own onboarding
competitors.note: The real competitor for small firms is often 'we'll figure it out ourselves'.

ideas.pricing: Swedish AI consultants are typically quoted at 1,200–2,500 SEK/h (Opsio). Tool seats cost roughly 200–700 SEK per user per month. A half-day team workshop is the easiest first sale.
risks: Knowledge goes stale within months. Answer: sell outcomes and a quarterly refresh retainer, not a one-off course. Teach the method (pick a task, redesign it, measure), which stays useful whichever tool wins.
The window may close in 3–5 years as vendors (Copilot, Gemini in Workspace) build onboarding into the tools
Firms under 20 staff are adopting slowly, so they're the hardest to sell to; 20–250 staff is the sweet spot
Mostly a sales job: meetings, follow-ups, proposals
Conflict of interest or contract terms with your current employer: check before selling on the side
ideas.next: Run one internal pilot at work: pick one team and one painful workflow, measure hours before and after, and write it up as a one-page case study. Target 20–250 person firms after that.

41% of workers say employer did nothing to prepare them
Pax8: shadow AI in small businesses

market: Sweden 2025 (SCB): 35% of firms with 10+ staff use some AI, up from 25% in 2024. By size: small (10–49) 30.8%, medium 49.6%, large 71.9%.
65% of Swedish firms used no AI in 2025, and 57.9% neither used it nor considered it.
Among Swedish firms that considered AI but didn't adopt it, the top reason was lack of relevant expertise (74.7%).
The EU average is 20% (2025), up from 13.5% in 2024. Sweden is third behind Denmark (42%) and Finland (37.8%).
US (Census, 2026): about 18–20% of firms use AI. Use is rising at firms with 20+ staff but is flat at firms under 20.
Depth: most big companies use AI somewhere, but only about a third are scaling it. 48% added AI without redesigning the workflow (Deloitte 2026), and only 12% have redesigned at scale.

Workers are ahead of their employers: 89% use AI at work (Study.com), 41% say their employer gave no tools, training or guidance (Resume Now), and 35% of AI-using SMBs found unapproved AI running in their business (Pax8).
The gap is between individual use (high) and company adoption (low). The bottleneck is expertise and workflow redesign, not access to tools.

ideas.name: Footage logger for wedding videographers
ideas.pitch: Upload a day of clips and get a searchable inventory, transcripts of speeches and vows, and a beat-timed rough cut list.
ideas.verdict: Strong edge: you've already built the core for two wedding films. Needs competitor research, since editing suites are adding AI features fast.
edge: Working pipeline from the Jennie & Gunnar and Emma projects
You understand how an editor actually works through a wedding day
risks: Premiere, DaVinci Resolve and Descript may ship the same features as part of their own products
ideas.next: Desk research: what do Premiere, Resolve, Descript and the AI-first editing tools already do? Then ask three videographers how they log a wedding today.

ideas.name: Burned-in subtitles to editable .srt
ideas.pitch: Turn a video with hard-coded subtitles back into an editable subtitle file, for indie filmmakers, translators and festival submissions.
ideas.verdict: You've already built it once (Tomma Händer). The problem is real but occasional, which may make it better as a free tool that builds an audience than as a product people pay for.
risks: Free OCR tools already exist, at lower quality
ideas.next: Check existing tools and their quality. Consider releasing it free as an audience-builder.

ideas.name: Bespoke event and trip microsites
ideas.pitch: Memorable private sites for bachelorettes, weddings, reunions and birthdays: schedules, inside jokes, secret gates, slideshows.
ideas.verdict: Fun, fast to sell to friends-of-friends, and a strong portfolio. It's a want, not a pain, so it's priced as a gift. It probably won't scale beyond word of mouth.
edge: Emma bachelorette, Trung Thu and the Callback CV as a portfolio
risks: Wedding website builders (Zola, The Knot, Joy) are free
Every site is custom work, so it's hard to scale
ideas.next: Ask everyone who saw the Emma site whether they'd have paid for one, and how much.

ideas.name: Tết as a guest in a Vietnamese village
ideas.pitch: Small groups of westerners spend Tết as guests of a real family in the countryside: wrapping bánh chưng, the market run, lì xì. Like being brought home for midsommar.
ideas.verdict: This is access, not an itinerary, and access is what can't be copied. The hard part is keeping it organic: guests, not tourists, with roles to play, paying hosts properly, small groups, saying no often. It only happens once a year, so it's a premium experience, not an income. It doubles as writing material.
edge: You can brief guests on both cultures
The festival happens regardless, so it's authentic by default
risks: Feeling commercial ruins it for both hosts and guests
Once a year, with a hard deadline
Tết is also the most expensive and crowded time to travel
ideas.next: Tết 2027 is 6 Feb. Run a free or at-cost pilot with 2–4 friends or colleagues, document it, and ask them afterwards what they would have paid.

ideas.name: Custom Vietnam itineraries
ideas.pitch: Tailored, exclusive itineraries for westerners in or visiting Vietnam.
ideas.verdict: AI makes generic itineraries free, and agencies and bloggers already cover this. It only survives as an add-on to something exclusive, like the Tết village.
risks: Sales and marketing heavy, which you said is your weak spot
ideas.next: Park it. Fold the useful parts into the Tết idea.

ideas.name: Build in public (the viral engine)
ideas.pitch: Share the weird, specific things you build with AI. The audience becomes the distribution channel for every other idea.
ideas.verdict: Not a business on its own, but it solves the sales problem that every other idea has. Score it as an enabler, not a money-maker.
edge: A backlog of real, shareable builds
ideas.next: Pick one platform and one format. Post the drill-beat wedding cut story as the first test.
